title: Experts on “voter fraud” in Sweden: Nothing indicates that it is happening deliberately
content:
In recent weeks, claims of electoral fraud have appeared on social media. But what has happened, and does everything being highlighted really constitute electoral fraud? NORDIS partner Källkritikbyrån examine a few examples with political scientists.

“It’s voter fraud,” says Malmölistan party leader Nils Littorin as he walks around looking for his party’s ballot papers at a polling station. The video, posted on X two weeks ago, has been viewed nearly 350,000 times.

Video on X on 26 August.

“It’s probably some private individual who took the ballot papers,” one person says in the comments.

Nils Littorin replies: “Damn it, that’s electoral fraud just the same. It doesn’t matter WHO does it. Keep fighting to defend the fraud.”

Since early voting began this year, there have been several claims of electoral fraud on social media. Among other things, several small parties have posted videos in which election officials are accused of failing to put out ballot papers for all parties in the screened-off areas. Others have reported being turned away when they tried to vote while wearing clothing displaying political propaganda.

creator: Matilda Nilsson
sourceDescription: The Nordic Observatory for Digital Media and Information Disorder

title: Rumours of voter fraud spread after voting problems in Sweden
content:
“Voter fraud everywhere,” a person wrote on X about advance votes that were incorrectly registered. But the Swedish Election Authority rejects the claim, NORDIS partner Källkritikbyrån reports.

Last Friday the Swedish Election Authority reported a technical error that was then feared to affect approximately 4,000 advance votes. Over the weekend, the error concerning advance votes was analysed, and it was found that at most 500 advance votes are affected.

The figure may decrease further, the Swedish Election Authority writes on its website, and regrets that it will probably not be possible to determine who cast these votes.

– The error occurred because election officials began accepting a new vote before they had completed the voting process for the previous voter. As a result, the votes were registered incorrectly, Jenny Stad, press officer at the Swedish Election Authority, told Källkritikbyrån.

Post on X on 4 September.
snippet: “Voter fraud everywhere,” a person wrote on X about advance votes that were incorrectly registered. But the Swedish Election Authority rejects the claim, NORDIS partner Källkritikbyrån reports.
creator: Matilda Nilsson
sourceDescription: The Nordic Observatory for Digital Media and Information Disorder

title: Misinformation emerges as Sweden’s election run-up goes into final stage
content:
NORDIS and its Swedish partners Källkritikbyrån and Fojo Media Institute examine how misinformation, AI and election fraud rumours are shaping the Swedish election campaign.

The Swedish election campaign for municipal, regional and national elections is in full swing, marking the beginning of a high season for potential misinformation in Sweden.

NORDIS has spoken to its partners at fact-checking organisation Källkritikbyrån and the Fojo Media Institute at Linnaeus University about the role misinformation has played in the Swedish election campaign so far.

Sweden is an easy target in the information space, because of its reputation as a liberal country. This means both positively, as a perceived successful progressive society and negatively, where it’s claimed to be wrecked by immigrants or too “woke”.
snippet: NORDIS and its Swedish partners Källkritikbyrån and Fojo Media Institute examine how misinformation, AI and election fraud rumours are shaping the Swedish election campaign.
creator: Andreas Oved Askjær Rasmussen
sourceDescription: The Nordic Observatory for Digital Media and Information Disorder

title: New project to support newsrooms against disinformation ahead of Swedish election
content:
Alerts about AI-generated content, independent fact-checking and dedicated support for smaller newsrooms. The project Valkollen 2026 (“The Election Check”) aims to equip Swedish journalists ahead of the upcoming general election. The initiative is led by NORDIS partner Fojo Media Institute at Linnaeus University and made possible by a donation of four million Swedish kronor.

“Ahead of the 2026 election, journalists will face an information landscape where the pace is relentless, the flows overwhelming and attempts at manipulative influence more sophisticated than ever. Valkollen 2026 gives Swedish journalists the tools to counter attempts to manipulate public opinion,” says Andreas Önnerfors, researcher at NORDIS partner Fojo Media Institute and project manager for Valkollen 2026, a project under the umbrella of the Fojo Verify section of the Institute.

title: Hoaxes and misleading claims in the Swedish election campaign
content:
AI-generated clickbait, fake election posters and classic half-truths from politicians – here is NORDIS partner Källkritikbyrån’s major review of the election campaign’s hoaxes and distortions.

Fact-checkers such as Källkritikbyrån and the Valkollen project are monitoring the Swedish election and looking for false and misleading claims. The election campaign is now entering its final stage – here NORDIS partner Källkritikbyrån review what has emerged so far.

Clickbait networks make money from ad clicks during election periods

Excerpt from a Facebook post on 18 May.

Källkritikbyrån has previously exposed a network of Facebook pages that share false and inflammatory content to drive traffic to “news sites” filled with advertisements. The actors behind them include people in Vietnam, who use the method to make money. Last year, the content consisted of AI-generated sob stories, but in January we discovered that the pages were also involving themselves in the case of a missing 18-year-old in Uddevalla and spreading false claims.
snippet: AI-generated clickbait, fake election posters and classic half-truths from politicians – here is NORDIS partner Källkritikbyrån’s major review of the election campaign’s hoaxes and distortions.
creator: Matilda Nilsson
sourceDescription: The Nordic Observatory for Digital Media and Information Disorder

title: Election Authority on ID concerns online: “Never heard of it happening”
content:
The Election Authority’s information that you can vote without ID – if another person with identification vouches for you – has surprised and stirred emotions on social media. But it is actually the result of a tightening of the law 20 years ago, the Swedish fact-checking media outlet and NORDIS partner Källkritikbyrån reports.

A post published on Twitter/X on Monday reads: “What the fuck is this shit? It’s like asking for election fraud”. The post has so far been viewed more than 163,000 times according to the platform’s counter.

Attached is an image of the Election Authority’s information sheet, with a paragraph marked in red:

You do not need to bring your voting card in order to vote. But you need to bring an ID document. If you do not have an ID document, another person can certify that you are you. That person must show their ID document.

From screenshot on Twitter/X of the Election Authority’s information sheet

title: Google’s AI Overview is still spewing false information about AI images – sources include Russian media, a crypto site and Reddit
content:
Google’s AI Overview still does not reliably assess photographs created with artificial intelligence. The reliability of AI Overviews is a particularly topical issue now, as a German court found in June that Google and other AI companies are responsible for errors in AI Overviews.

This is the conclusion of an analysis by the Finish NORDIS partner, Faktabaari.

Google’s AI Overview connected to reverse image search is a highly unreliable tool for assessing AI images.

Faktabaari tested in April 2026 how often Google’s AI Overview provides correct information about AI images entered into Google’s reverse image search. The result was worrying. In Finnish-language tests, the AI provided completely correct information only once out of ten. In a Swedish-language test repeated later, correct information was provided slightly more often: four times out of ten.

Google, commenting on the test result to Faktabaari, promised to take “action in accordance with our policies as necessary”.

title: Investigation: Russia recruits young “agents” on social media
content:
It is well known that criminal networks in recent years have recruited children and young teenagers through social media. But they are not the only ones who have operated in this way.

State actors have also recently used online platforms to recruit young people to commit acts of terrorism, violence and vandalism in the West in return for payment.

In September, almost a year ago, two 17-year-old Dutch boys were arrested for carrying out services for a foreign country.

The boys are believed to have been recruited by pro-Russian agents or hackers on Telegram. One of them is believed to have been charged with spying on Europol, Eurojust and the Canadian embassy in The Hague by using a “wifi sniffer”, a device that can pick up nearby wifi networks.

More complex and unpredictable

The recruits are described by The Financial Times (FT) as “disposable” agents who pose little risk to the state itself and are easy to replace. They are often young people who are contacted on social media such as Telegram, TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook or Discord and offered money in return for carrying out assignments.
snippet: It is well known that criminal networks in recent years have recruited children and young teenagers through social media. But they are not the only ones who have operated in this way.
creator: Kajsa Garmann Lønrusten
sourceDescription: The Nordic Observatory for Digital Media and Information Disorder

title: Global Fact summit: Countering authoritarian influence with quality journalism
content:
This year’s Global Fact event in Vilnius offered a broad showcase of the expertise of fact-checkers and investigative journalists. The major American digital platforms no longer participated in the event. We have compiled the main takeaways from the conference in this article.

Fact-checkers gathered during Midsummer week for the 13th international Global Fact summit in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. The political upheavals of recent years were reflected both in the composition of the event and in its themes. The presentations focused on the impact of artificial intelligence on information disorders and on democracies’ information defence against authoritarian influence.

There were somewhat fewer participants than before, as many newsrooms specialising in fact-checking have ceased their operations after the American digital giants Meta and Google’s owner Alphabet cut back on fact-checking across their social media services at the beginning of last year.

In the current political situation, responsibility for fact-checking and defending the integrity of the information environment is increasingly falling to European actors.

title: NORDIS partner wins international award for impactful investigation
content:
NORDIS’ Danish fact-checking partner TjekDet has won the international “Global Fact-Checking Award 2026” together with the Danish newspaper Politiken, the Dutch outlet Bellingcat, and the Canadian broadcaster CBC at the award ceremony in Vilnius for their investigation exposing the person behind MrDeepFakes.

When the four media outlets published the investigation, MrDeepFakes was the world’s largest website for deepfake pornography, where well-known people – almost always women – were manipulated into pornographic videos with the help of artificial intelligence.

Among the victims were actors, TV presenters, influencers, and politicians.

The investigation led to the website shutting down in May last year. Before that, it was visited by several million users every single month.

“When we began this work, it was not only about finding the man behind the world’s largest deepfake pornography website. Above all, it was about the thousands of people whose faces, identities, and privacy were abused without their consent. That is why it means a great deal to us that this particular story is now being recognised internationally,” says TjekDet Editor-in-Chief Thomas Hedin.
